body.text: In November 2024, a month after North Korea sent the first batch of 12,000 troops to Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed that Pyongyang could send up to 100,000 troops. Zelenskyy doubled down on this claim in December after North Korea was reported to have suffered from 3,000 casualties. In July 2025, Ukraine was reported to be anticipating another 30,000 North Korean troops more to bolster Russia’s defence. In August this year, Zelenskyy revised his estimate once more, saying he now expected 50,000 North Korean soldiers to be deployed to Russia.

But the problem with Ukraine’s forecasts is these larger troop deployments have never eventuated. The estimated number of North Korean troops in Russia remains between 14,000 and 16,000 – higher than the 12,000 from the initial deployment in October 2024, but a discrepancy explained by different methods of estimation among Ukrainian, South Korea, and Western intelligence agencies. North Korea has largely stopped sending more troops since late 2024. The South Korean military doesn’t detect any signs of future deployment.

North Korea’s pause is worth noting. It was North Korean Chairman Kim Jong-un’s idea to send troops to Russia to repel Ukraine’s invasion of Kursk. As the war drags on, Russia needs personnel and is expanding recruitment to Africa. Moscow could have asked North Korea to dispatch more troops to defend the Russian frontline – but there is no sign of that occurring.
Sending labourers, by contrast, earns the regime hard currency without putting them in harm’s way.

Of the North Korean soldiers still stationed in Russia, 9,500 are deployed as active duty and are engaged with firing barrel artillery and multiple launch rocket systems against Ukrainian forces along the Russia–Ukraine border in the Kursk region. These soldiers are also conducting reconnaissance and attack drone operations. Pyongyang has also sent labourers to assemble drones in weapons factories and to rebuild war-torn Kursk. Each North Korean labourer in Russia is believed to earn US$7,500 per year, much less than the US$24,000 that a soldier makes for the state.

There have not been any breakthroughs on the diplomatic front to justify the pause in North Korean troop deployments. North Korea continues to reject dialogue with the United States and South Korea, while Russia keeps shelling Ukrainian cities. The Russia–North Korea arms trade valued at US$14.4 billion remains robust , which suggests there has been no alliance quarrel. China has not criticised North Korean troop deployment to Russia and is keen to expand economic cooperation with Pyongyang.

Instead, the pause in North Korean deployments seems to be due to the changing nature of the Russia–Ukraine war. Ukraine’s counteroffensive now centres on recapturing Russia-held territory in the Donetsk Oblast instead of occupying Russian ground. It has not launched any attacks on Russian territory since withdrawing from Kursk in March 2025. North Korea doesn’t allow its soldiers to fight on Ukrainian soil because the scope of its alliance treaty with Russia doesn’t cover Ukraine, including land under Russian de facto control. Ukraine and Russia have also shifted to using long-range missiles and drones to attack targets deep behind the frontline. North Korean troops have little air defence capability to offer Russia.

The pause also sheds light on what happened on the North Korean homefront. The domestic audience, even in a highly controlled state, must still be considered. When North Korea first dispatched troops in October 2024, it neither confirmed nor denied the move. North Korea kept its deployment a secret, issuing death certificates for soldiers killed in Russia as having died “in training”. Pyongyang only admitted to casualties in April 2025 after news had spread throughout the country and Ukraine had withdrawn from Kursk. The recent capture and handover of two North Korean soldiers by Ukraine to South Korea was also an indication of defection risks if North Korea sent too many new recruits at once. Deploying additional troops to Russia without the ability to reintegrate them back to society can undermine the government’s control on outside information. Poor treatment of veterans or killed soldiers’ families can be equally dangerous.

North Korea doesn’t need to send additional troops to have achieved the main objectives with Russia. Its soldiers have gained real combat experience and can teach those skills in military academies at home. Pyongyang has demonstrated the efficiency of its weapons on the Russian battlefield to prospective buyers. And it has also fulfilled its end of the alliance contract by defending Kursk, which Moscow repays by sharing sensitive military technology.

Sending labourers, by contrast, earns the regime hard currency without putting them in harm’s way. These labourers also provide North Korea with first-hand expertise if it wants to modernise the domestic military industry.
It seems likely North Korea will rely on the 9,500 active soldiers still on Russian soil to meet its defence obligations. Don’t expect that number to go up anytime soon.
Khang Vu is a visiting researcher in the Political Science Department at Boston College.
